script.opening_words:
It's the first of the month and Linda
sits at her kitchen table with a coffee
gone cold doing math nobody warned her
about. Her social security landed this
morning, $1,900 same as last month, same
as next, next to a Medicare letter that
just nudged her Part B premium up again
and the grocery coupons. In her head is
last week's headline, "The average
retiree supposedly has $600,000."
Linda worked 41 years, raised two kids,
never missed a payment.
script.ending_words:
o, if today
landed heavy, I want you to sit with
this instead. None of these numbers are
verdict on you. They are a map of a
system that pulled the pension, handed
you the risk, and then had the nerve to
call you irresponsible for being nervous
about it. You do not have to be the
average. The average is a ghost. You're
a real person sitting at a real table
who can run real numbers, and that
honestly already puts you miles ahead of
almost everyone who ever scrolled past
that headline and just believed it. So,
go find your number, not the headlines,
yours. I'm Nick. I'll see you in the
next one.
script.analysis: All 17,293 stored characters read in two contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Composite Linda (Social Security $1,900, $110K saved, Part B letter) frames the whole video and returns at the end. Sections: SCF mean $609K vs median $200K for 65-74 with a "Bezos walks into a bar" analogy; 4% rule on $200K; Fidelity 401k millionaires vs ~$30K median; 2026 average Social Security ~$2,071; dependence shares; 2033 trust-fund depletion and 77% payable; Northwestern Mutual $1.26M magic number vs $185K near-retiree median; gender and racial gaps; Fidelity $172,500 healthcare estimate, long-term care odds and nursing-home costs; Part B premium vs COLA; retiree credit-card debt; plan-to-work vs actual and forced early retirement; DB pension decline; mid-late "faceless YouTube channel" community CTA; actions (claiming age, HSA, pay off 22% cards, know your number); empathetic close. Well-structured, empathetic, mostly sourced to named organizations; one internal numeric contradiction and conditional-statistic framing issues. ASR not audio-verified.

claim_audit: 0:8700 SCF 2022 retirement-account mean ~$609K and median $200K for ages 65-74 and median ~$185K for 55-64 match Federal Reserve figures, but they are conditional on families that hold retirement accounts; the script says "every household", omitting that roughly half have none, so typical household savings are lower than presented. $200,000 x 4% = $8,000/year = ~$667/month correct. 2026 average retired-worker benefit ~$2,071 consistent with SSA after the 2.8% COLA. "About 4 in 10" majority-dependent and "1 in 7" at 90%+ consistent with SSA fact-sheet ranges.

0:8700 2025 Trustees: combined/OASI reserves depleted ~2033 with ~77% payable consistent; typical-couple cut ~$16,500 resembles CRFB estimates (latest versions somewhat higher), unverified exact. Northwestern Mutual 2025 "magic number" $1.26M consistent with the 2025 study; $1.26M / $185K = ~6.8x ("about 1/7") correct. Fidelity 401k median "closer to $30,000" is approximate (industry medians ~$35-40K).

8700:17293 Fidelity 2025 estimate $172,500 single / ~$345,000 couple consistent. Contradiction: script says $172,000 is "more than six times the median retirement balance of someone 75 and older", then states the median 75-year-old has $130,000 (SCF 2022, conditional) - ratio ~1.3x. Long-term care "~70% chance" is a widely cited HHS figure (newer estimates lower, ~56% for some care); private nursing room >$100K/year consistent with Genworth-type surveys. 2026 Part B premium increase exceeded the 2.8% COLA, consistent.

8700:17293 EBRI Retirement Confidence Survey patterns (about 3/4 workers expect to work in retirement vs ~1/3 retirees did; expected 65 vs actual ~62; ~4 in 10 retiring early for health) consistent with recent releases. Private-sector DB coverage decline is real, but "six in 10 covered workers in early 1980s to ~4% today" mixes coverage definitions; unverified. "$180,000 lifetime cost of claiming at the wrong time" resembles a 2019 United Income analysis (reported figures vary by household definition); unverified. HSA triple tax advantage correct federally (some states tax HSAs).
